questions.q: In the realistic order an on-call engineer follows during an incident, what does a metric alert typically tell you first?
options: The exact line of code that failed
That something is wrong and roughly when it started, without yet knowing what or where
The full stack trace of the error
Nothing useful without logs
questions.explain: Metrics are the first signal — a dashboard crossing a threshold tells you something is wrong and approximately when, which is the starting point for digging into logs and then traces.

questions.q: What field has to appear in both a log line and its matching trace for correlation to work?
options: The server's hostname
The same trace_id value
The HTTP status code
The log level
questions.explain: A shared trace_id is what links a specific log line to the specific trace (and spans) that were active when it was written, enabling a direct jump between the two signals.

questions.q: How do most OpenTelemetry SDKs get a trace ID into application log lines?
options: Developers must manually copy the trace ID into every log statement
When a log statement executes inside an active span, the SDK automatically stamps that span's trace ID onto the log record
Trace IDs are never present in logs — only in traces
A separate database maps logs to traces after the fact
questions.explain: Most language SDKs inject the active span's trace ID into log output automatically, which is what makes a one-click jump from a log line to its trace possible.

questions.q: In the Northbridge flash-sale example, what did the trace ultimately reveal that the metric alert alone could not?
options: That the alert was a false positive
That a mysql SELECT nested under an exhausted database connection pool, not the payment gateway, was the actual slow step
That no services were involved in the request
That the issue was caused by a DNS outage
questions.explain: The latency metric only showed that checkout was slow overall; the trace waterfall pinpointed the exact span — a database query under a connection pool bottleneck — responsible for the delay.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe correlation as something you get 'for free' rather than a fourth tool to buy?
options: Because correlation tools are always free of charge
Because it naturally follows once structured logging, centralized log search, and tracing are already implemented correctly
Because correlation requires no trace IDs at all
Because metrics, logs, and traces are stored in the same database automatically by default
questions.explain: Correlation is the payoff of doing the groundwork right: structured logs with a trace ID field, a centralized place to search them, and a tracing system producing those IDs — not a separate product.
